output.summary: Sequence transduction tasks such as machine translation were dominated by recurrent encoder-decoder networks, whose step-by-step computation over positions prevents parallelism within a training example and forces information between distant words to travel through many steps. This paper proposes the Transformer, an encoder-decoder architecture that drops recurrence and convolution and relies only on attention: scaled dot-product attention, run as several parallel heads, used for self-attention in the encoder and decoder and for encoder-decoder attention. Position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections with layer normalization, and sinusoidal positional encodings complete the design, the encodings supplying word order. The authors argue that self-attention connects any two positions in a constant number of sequential operations and is cheaper per layer than recurrence when sequences are shorter than the representation dimension. They back this with state-of-the-art BLEU on WMT 2014 English-German (28.4) and English-French, reached at a fraction of earlier training costs. Ablations show which components matter, and a constituency-parsing experiment suggests the architecture transfers beyond translation. This matters because it showed that attention alone, which parallelizes well on GPUs, can replace recurrence in sequence models.
main_claims: A sequence transduction model can dispense with recurrence and convolution entirely and rely only on attention, and doing so gives better translation quality.

Scaled dot-product attention, softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V, is fast because it is just matrix multiplication; the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling keeps large dot products from pushing the softmax into regions with tiny gradients.

Multi-head attention, several lower-dimensional attention heads run in parallel and concatenated, lets the model attend to different representation subspaces at once, which a single averaging head inhibits, at roughly the same cost as one full-dimensional head.

Self-attention layers need O(1) sequential operations and have O(1) maximum path length between any two positions, against O(n) for recurrent layers, which makes training more parallel and should make long-range dependencies easier to learn.

The Transformer sets new state-of-the-art BLEU on WMT 2014 English-German (28.4) and English-French (big model) at a small fraction of competitors' training cost, and it generalizes to English constituency parsing.
background: Feed-forward neural networks, linear layers and the ReLU activation
Training by gradient descent and backpropagation
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs/LSTMs) and their hidden-state recurrence
Word embeddings: mapping tokens to learned vectors
The softmax function and the dot product of vectors
Dropout and the idea of overfitting
The BLEU score as a machine translation quality metric (at the level of 'higher is better')

sections.label: motivation-recurrence
sections.title: The problem with recurrence and the idea of attention-only models
key_points: Recurrent models compute hidden state h_t from h_{t-1} and input t, so computation within one training example is inherently sequential and cannot be parallelized across positions.

This sequential constraint becomes critical at longer sequence lengths because memory limits how much batching across examples can compensate; factorization tricks and conditional computation help but do not remove it.
Attention mechanisms already let models relate positions regardless of distance, but were almost always used together with an RNN.

Convolutional alternatives (Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, ConvS2S) compute in parallel, but the number of operations needed to relate two distant positions grows with their distance: linearly for ConvS2S, logarithmically for ByteNet.

The Transformer reduces this to a constant number of operations, at the cost of reduced effective resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions, which multi-head attention is meant to counteract.

Self-attention (intra-attention) relates different positions of a single sequence to compute a representation of that sequence; the authors claim the Transformer is the first transduction model built entirely on it.

sections.label: architecture-overview
sections.title: Encoder-decoder architecture, residuals and masking
key_points: The encoder maps input symbols (x1..xn) to continuous representations z; the decoder generates outputs (y1..ym) one at a time, auto-regressively feeding back previously generated symbols.
The encoder is a stack of N=6 identical layers, each with a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a position-wise feed-forward sub-layer.

Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), a residual connection followed by layer normalization, and all sub-layers and embeddings output vectors of dimension d_model = 512 so the residual additions work.
The decoder also has 6 layers, adding a third sub-layer that attends over the encoder output.

The decoder's self-attention is masked so positions cannot attend to later positions; together with output embeddings shifted right by one, this ensures the prediction for position i depends only on outputs before i.

sections.label: scaled-dot-product-attention
sections.title: Scaled dot-product attention
key_points: An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output that is a weighted sum of the values, with weights given by the compatibility of the query with each key.
Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V, processing all queries at once as matrices.

Dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention (a one-hidden-layer feed-forward network), because it uses optimized matrix multiplication code, although the two have similar theoretical complexity.
Without scaling, additive attention outperforms dot-product attention for large d_k; the authors suspect large dot products push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients.
If the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance d_k, which motivates dividing by sqrt(d_k).

sections.label: multi-head-attention
sections.title: Multi-head attention and its three uses
key_points: Multi-head attention projects Q, K and V h times with different learned linear projections, runs attention in parallel on each, concatenates the h outputs and projects them again with W^O.
Multiple heads let the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions; with a single head, averaging inhibits this.
The paper uses h=8 heads with d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64, so the total cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality.
In encoder-decoder attention, queries come from the previous decoder layer and keys and values from the encoder output, so every decoder position can attend to all input positions.
In encoder self-attention, Q, K and V all come from the previous encoder layer, and each position attends to all positions.
In decoder self-attention, illegal leftward connections are masked by setting their softmax inputs to minus infinity, which preserves the auto-regressive property.

sections.label: ffn-embeddings-positions
sections.title: Feed-forward layers, embeddings and positional encoding
key_points: Each layer contains a position-wise feed-forward network FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2, applied identically to every position (like two convolutions with kernel size 1), with inner dimension d_ff = 2048.

Learned embeddings map tokens to d_model-dimensional vectors; the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear layer share one weight matrix, and the embedding weights are multiplied by sqrt(d_model).
Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, it has no notion of order unless position information is injected; positional encodings of dimension d_model are added to the input embeddings.
The encodings use sines and cosines of different frequencies, with wavelengths in a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π.
The authors hypothesized sinusoids make attending by relative position easy, because PE_{pos+k} is a linear function of PE_pos for any fixed offset k.
Learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results; sinusoids were chosen because they may extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training.

sections.label: why-self-attention
sections.title: Why self-attention: complexity, parallelism and path length
key_points: Layer types are compared on three criteria: total computation per layer, the minimum number of sequential operations (parallelizability), and the maximum path length between any two positions.

Per Table 1, self-attention costs O(n²·d) per layer with O(1) sequential operations and O(1) path length; recurrent layers cost O(n·d²) with O(n) sequential operations and O(n) path length; convolutional layers cost O(k·n·d²) with O(log_k n) path length when dilated.
Self-attention is cheaper than recurrence when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimension d, which is the usual case for sentence-level word-piece or byte-pair representations.
Shorter paths between positions are argued to make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
For very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to a neighborhood of size r, raising the maximum path length to O(n/r); the authors leave this for future work.
As a side benefit, attention distributions can be inspected, and individual heads appear to learn different tasks related to syntax and semantics.

sections.label: training-setup
sections.title: Training regime: data, schedule, optimizer and regularization
key_points: English-German used WMT 2014 (about 4.5M sentence pairs) with a shared byte-pair vocabulary of about 37000 tokens; English-French used 36M sentences with a 32000 word-piece vocabulary; batches held about 25000 source and 25000 target tokens.
Training ran on one machine with 8 P100 GPUs: base models for 100K steps (12 hours, about 0.4 s per step) and big models for 300K steps (3.5 days, 1.0 s per step).
Adam was used (β1=0.9, β2=0.98, ε=1e-9) with a learning rate that rises linearly over the first 4000 warmup steps and then decays with the inverse square root of the step number.
Residual dropout (P_drop = 0.1 for the base model) is applied to each sub-layer output before the residual addition and to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings.
Label smoothing with ε_ls = 0.1 hurts perplexity because the model learns to be more unsure, but it improves accuracy and BLEU.

sections.label: translation-results
sections.title: Machine translation results and training cost
key_points: On WMT 2014 English-German, Transformer (big) reaches 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 BLEU above the best previous models including ensembles, and even the base model (27.3) beats all previous models and ensembles.

On English-French, the big model sets a new single-model state of the art at less than 1/4 the training cost of the previous best; Table 2 lists 41.8 BLEU, while the text of Section 6.1 says 41.0, an inconsistency in the paper itself.
Training costs in FLOPs are estimates computed as training time × number of GPUs × assumed sustained GPU throughput; for example, the base model's 3.3·10^18 is far below competitors' 10^19–10^21.
Results use checkpoint averaging (last 5 checkpoints for base, last 20 for big) and beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6.

sections.label: ablations
sections.title: Model variations: which components matter
key_points: Ablations vary the base model on the newstest2013 development set, without checkpoint averaging, reporting per-wordpiece perplexity and BLEU.
Rows (A): at constant computation, single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting (24.9 vs 25.8), and quality also drops with too many heads (32 heads: 25.4).

Rows (B): reducing the key size d_k hurts quality, which the authors read as a sign that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than the dot product might help.
Rows (C) and (D): bigger models do better (for example d_model = 1024 gives 26.0 BLEU), and dropout matters (P_drop = 0 gives 24.6 BLEU).
Row (E): learned positional embeddings perform nearly identically to sinusoids (25.7 vs 25.8 BLEU).
The big configuration (d_model = 1024, d_ff = 4096, h = 16, P_drop = 0.3, 300K steps, 213M parameters) reaches 26.4 dev BLEU, against 25.8 for the 65M-parameter base model.

sections.label: parsing-generalization
sections.title: Generalization to English constituency parsing
key_points: Constituency parsing is a hard test because its output is strongly structured and much longer than its input, and RNN sequence-to-sequence models had not reached state of the art in small-data regimes.

A 4-layer Transformer with d_model = 1024 was trained on WSJ (about 40K sentences) and semi-supervised on about 17M sentences, with only a small number of experiments to select dropout, learning rates and beam size.

It scores 91.3 F1 with WSJ only and 92.7 semi-supervised, better than all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar; Table 4's multi-task (93.0) and generative (93.3) entries are listed separately.
Unlike RNN sequence-to-sequence models, it outperforms the BerkeleyParser even when trained only on the 40K WSJ sentences.

sections.label: attention-visualizations-conclusion
sections.title: Attention visualizations and conclusions
key_points: Visualizations from encoder self-attention in layer 5 of 6 show heads following long-distance dependencies, for example 'making' attending to 'more difficult'.

Two heads appear to perform anaphora resolution, attending sharply from 'its' to 'Law' and 'application'; other heads show behaviour that seems related to sentence structure, and different heads appear to learn different tasks.
These visualizations are a handful of examples presented qualitatively, as suggestive evidence of interpretability rather than a systematic analysis.
The authors conclude that attention-only models train significantly faster than recurrent or convolutional ones and set a new state of the art in translation.
Planned future work: other modalities such as images, audio and video, local restricted attention for large inputs, and making generation less sequential.
